tile-k1-04.title: Around the bend
tile-k1-04.instruction: Cover the path around the bend.
tile-k1-04.idea: A tricky shape may have an easy starting place.
hints: Find a square at a tip.
The bottom square can only reach upward.
Pair the left two squares up and down. Pair the two remaining top squares.

parent.notice: Watch for a switch between horizontal and vertical thinking.
parent.prompt: Which square helped you decide where to start?
parent.explanation: The bottom tip forces a vertical domino. The two remaining top squares then form a horizontal pair. This is the only complete tiling.
parent.extension: Turn a paper copy around. Does turning the whole board change its solution?
parent.connection: Local constraints can determine an entire matching.

tile-k1-08.title: The little boat
tile-k1-08.instruction: Cover the boat, tip to tip.
tile-k1-08.idea: A mirror can help us predict a matching move.
hints: Look at the two bottom corners.
Each bottom corner has just one neighbor.
Pair the bottom-left two and bottom-right two. Finish the top pair.

parent.notice: Notice whether your child finds matching moves on the two sides.
parent.prompt: If this side needs a domino, what might the other side need?
parent.explanation: Both bottom corners force horizontal pairs. The two top squares then pair with each other. Reflection preserves this single tiling.
parent.extension: Fold a paper drawing along the middle. Do the dominoes match across the fold?
parent.connection: Symmetry can simplify a constraint problem.

tile-k1-12.title: The tiny crown
tile-k1-12.idea: Explain why your choices must work.
hints: Find the two side tips.
Each side tip has only one partner.
Cover each side tip with its neighbor. Finish the top pair and the bottom pair.

parent.notice: Invite an explanation in pointing and gestures, not just words.
parent.prompt: Can you show why no other domino can cover this tip?
parent.explanation: The left and right tips force the two middle-row horizontal pairs. The top and bottom pairs are then forced. Listing these reasons proves the tiling is unique.
parent.extension: Ask your child to teach someone else which pair must come first.
parent.connection: A chain of unavoidable choices is a small proof.

tile-23-04.title: The offset terraces
tile-23-04.idea: Choose a split that leaves solvable pieces.
hints: Look at the top two rows as one terrace.
The bottom two rows form another terrace, shifted right.
Use three vertical dominoes in the top terrace and three in the bottom terrace.

parent.notice: The child can choose an imaginary boundary through a connected board.
parent.prompt: Which two small rectangles can you see?
parent.explanation: Splitting between rows two and three gives two 2 by 3 rectangles. Tiling those separately proves the whole board works. Some other solutions cross the split; our construction need not find every solution.
parent.extension: Find a solution that does cross the middle split, then compare it with the two-terrace method.
parent.connection: Decomposition proves existence without claiming uniqueness.

tile-23-08.title: The small diamond
tile-23-08.idea: The border shapes the choices inside.
hints: Each row has an even number of squares.
Pair squares across to make a first solution.
Cover the top pair, both middle rows in pairs, and the bottom pair.

parent.notice: After one solution, ask where a small change is possible.
parent.prompt: Which two dominoes could turn together inside a square?
parent.explanation: This is an Aztec diamond of order two. Its twelve cells have eight tilings. The horizontal construction is one, and local 2 by 2 flips produce others.
parent.extension: Draw several solutions and mark which dominoes stay near the same boundary.
parent.connection: Larger Aztec diamonds reveal striking patterns in random tilings.

tile-23-12.title: The rearranging courtyard
tile-23-12.instruction: Cover the courtyard. Then try a new pattern.
tile-23-12.idea: Solutions themselves can form a network.
hints: Start with a pattern you can repeat.
Two dominoes in a 2 by 2 square can turn together.
A first solution is two horizontal dominoes in each row.

parent.notice: Keep the puzzle goal simple; the rearrangement is an optional conversation.
parent.prompt: Can you make another solution by changing just two dominoes?
parent.explanation: There are 36 tilings of this 4 by 4 board. A local flip trades two parallel dominoes in a square for the other orientation. Recording tilings as dots and flips as links makes a new graph.
parent.extension: Draw three or four linked solutions. A theorem guarantees all tilings of a simply connected domino region are linked by such flips.
parent.connection: The move graph of tilings is a research object.

tile-45-04.title: The sloping ridge
tile-45-04.instruction: Cover the ridge while protecting the narrow ends.
tile-45-04.idea: Global completion may force central choices.
hints: The top row and bottom row each form a pair.
Look for more forced pairs after the ends are covered.
A complete construction puts dominoes across each row, working left to right.

parent.notice: This board has fewer solutions than its size may suggest.
parent.prompt: Which choices disappear after you cover the two narrow ends?
parent.explanation: Every row has even length, so horizontal pairing provides a tiling. Exhaustive enumeration finds only four tilings: the narrow border forces many choices that look flexible at first.
parent.extension: Try to find the small patches where changes are actually possible. Compare a large rectangle with the same area.
parent.connection: Boundary conditions can strongly restrict a tiling space.

tile-45-08.title: The Aztec garden
tile-45-08.instruction: Cover the diamond; notice choices near its border.
tile-45-08.idea: The shape of a region influences its typical tilings.
hints: Every row contains an even number of cells.
Horizontal pairs give an easy first tiling.
Pair left to right in each row, starting with the two-cell top row.

parent.notice: This small board invites a question about large families, not a claim about statistics from one play.
parent.prompt: If we drew many different tilings, which patterns might keep appearing?
parent.explanation: This order-three Aztec diamond has 24 cells and 64 tilings, verified by enumeration. Every tiling uses twelve dominoes, but orientations and positions vary.
parent.extension: Sketch several tilings. Large uniformly random Aztec diamonds have a disordered central region approaching a circle and ordered outer regions. A hand-chosen sample here is not uniform and this tiny board is not the limiting theorem.
parent.connection: A small counting question leads to random tilings and limit shapes.

tile-45-12.title: A whole world of tilings
tile-45-12.instruction: Cover the courtyard, then explore a small change.
tile-45-12.idea: Ask about all solutions and the paths between them.
hints: A repeated row pattern is a useful first solution.
Look for a full 2 by 2 patch covered by two dominoes.
Start with three horizontal dominoes in each row; a pair of neighboring rows contains places to flip.

parent.notice: Celebrate a new question after solving: how many, how connected, how typical?
parent.prompt: Could you reach every tiling by turning two dominoes at a time?
parent.explanation: This 4 by 6 rectangle has 281 tilings. A local flip exchanges the two tilings of a 2 by 2 patch. Because the board is simply connected, its tilings are connected by flips. A height function encodes the tiling as integer heights at grid vertices.
parent.extension: Draw a short path of flips. Advanced questions study shortest paths, efficient random sampling, and fluctuations of height functions on much larger boards; this MVP does not measure those quantities.
parent.connection: Thurston’s height viewpoint links local moves with global structure.
